screens.title: Introduction to Kanban
screens.narratorSegment: Kanban is a lightweight, practical approach to managing knowledge work that started in manufacturing and found a powerful second life in software and services. In this lesson you will learn why Kanban focuses on visualizing the workflow, limiting how much is in progress, and improving the way work flows from request to delivery. We will connect the four foundational principles — starting with what you do now, evolutionary change, respecting roles, and encouraging leadership at all levels — to six actionable practices like visualizing the board and setting WIP limits. You will see concrete examples, such as a content team's board, and common misconceptions, for instance thinking that WIP limits are the same as arbitrary quotas. By the end, you will understand when Kanban is a better fit than a time-boxed framework and how small experiments can move your team toward smoother delivery. Keep an eye on the visual cards illustrating board stages, WIP, and a traffic metaphor to build an intuitive picture of flow.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Introduction to Kanban
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to Kanban

A practical guide to Kanban's philosophy, its four principles, and the six practices that help teams visualize and improve flow.

16:9 HD Classroom
What you will understand
How Kanban visualizes workflow and why WIP limits improve delivery.
Why it matters
Teams reduce delays and handoff friction by seeing work and enforcing limits.
Who benefits
Support, operations, maintenance, content teams, and anywhere priorities change often.
How we'll practice
Design a Kanban board with WIP limits and write explicit policies for key columns.
Explore Key Topics
Principles
Start with what you do now, evolve incrementally, respect roles, and encourage leadership.
Practices
Visualize workflow, set WIP limits, manage flow, and make policies explicit.
When to use Kanban
Best where work arrives unpredictably or continuous delivery is required.
Visual metaphor
Backlog
Ideas waiting to be pulled
In Development (WIP 3)
Limited work reduces context switching
Testing
Watch for pileups as bottlenecks
Done
Completed and ready to deliver
Traffic metaphor: lanes are stages, cars are work items; WIP limits prevent jams.
Key Takeaway

Kanban brings visibility and focus. Start small, measure lead and cycle time, and evolve your process experimentally.

Quick example
A content team uses: Ideas | Writing (WIP 2) | Editing (WIP 1) | Review | Publishing (WIP 1) | Done. Writers can only move finished drafts when editing has capacity, forcing the team to resolve the editing bottleneck together.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this set of objectives you will see four specific, verifiable skills to target while learning Kanban. First, you will explain Kanban's origins and its core philosophy, which helps ground the practices in a real-world context and shows why visualizing flow matters. Second, you will identify and describe the four foundational principles of Kanban so you can evaluate how a team culture supports evolutionary change. Third, you will understand and apply the six core practices, with emphasis on visualizing workflow and limiting Work In Progress; these practices form the toolkit for daily use. Fourth, you will learn to differentiate Kanban from Scrum, noticing how continuous flow contrasts with time-boxed Sprints and what that difference means for planning and cadence. Each objective links a clear skill to a practical reason: you will be able to design a board, set WIP limits, and choose the right approach for your team. As you study, look for opportunities to practice small experiments rather than trying to change everything at once.

screens.title: Origins and Philosophy of Kanban
screens.narratorSegment: Kanban began as a scheduling system in Toyota's production system and later translated into knowledge work because of its focus on flow and visual control. At its core Kanban is a method to make work visible, constrain work in progress, and encourage incremental improvement. The philosophy is intentionally non-prescriptive: you start with your current process and evolve it, rather than ripping everything up and replacing roles. A concrete example is a software operations team that maps incident handling to a board and then adds limits so they finish incidents faster. A common misconception is that Kanban is merely a to-do board; it's not. The board is a diagnostic tool used with policies, metrics, and experiments to improve flow. In practice, you'll notice that the same card moving slowly through stages signals different problems: lack of skill in a stage, unclear acceptance criteria, or resource shortages. The takeaway is that Kanban pairs simple visual tools with evidence-based changes — you visualize to learn, then experiment and measure, and encourage leadership across the team to propose improvements. How might you start by mapping one process you use today?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Kanban is a visual, evolutionary method for improving flow by starting with existing processes and making small, measurable changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Origins and Philosophy
Core Concept

Origins and Philosophy of Kanban

A definition and simple analogy that links manufacturing origins to modern knowledge work.

Definition
A visual method to improve flow by making work visible, limiting WIP, and evolving processes incrementally.
Analogy
Like traffic lanes and cars: lanes are stages and cars are work items; limits prevent jams and speed the whole road.
Misconception check
A Kanban board is not just a to-do list. It's paired with policies, metrics, and experiments to change how work flows.
Concrete example
An operations team maps incident lifecycle: Reported → Triage → In Progress → Verification → Resolved. They set a WIP limit on Triage and In Progress to two items each. When triage has two items, no more incidents are pulled until one advances. This revealed that verification lacked automation, so the team added a check to reduce verification time.
Key Takeaway
Start where you are, visualize to learn, then run small experiments to improve flow.
Try this
Map one routine process you run today and name three stages. That map is your starting board.

screens.title: Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part A
screens.narratorSegment: Two of Kanban's most distinctive principles help teams adopt changes with minimal disruption. First, 'Start with what you do now' asks you to map your existing workflow, roles, and responsibilities without requiring immediate structural changes. The practical benefit is lower resistance: team members keep their roles and still gain visibility. For example, a support team might leave existing escalation paths in place while introducing a simple board to track incoming tickets. Second, 'Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change' emphasizes making small, measurable experiments rather than large overhauls. A concrete experiment could be changing a WIP limit for one column to see whether lead time improves. A common error is to misread evolutionary change as slow or vague; in fact it's deliberate and measurable. Each small change should have a hypothesis, a way to measure lead or cycle time, and a review loop. These two principles combined make Kanban adoptable in environments where stability of roles is important, and they prioritize learning over assumption. Think of each experiment as a tiny scientific trial: small, safe, and information-rich. Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part A means begin with the current process and make deliberate, incremental changes measured by simple metrics.. In practical terms, start with what you do now and pursue evolutionary change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Four Foundational Principles — Part A
Principle

Start with what you do now

Map your current workflow and keep existing roles while adding visibility and small process rules.

Why this matters
It reduces resistance and allows immediate transparency without restructuring teams.
Example
A support team keeps existing escalations but adds columns for Triage and In Progress to see backlog shape.
Principle

Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change

Choose small, measurable experiments and observe their effect on flow rather than doing a large transformation.

How to experiment
Set a hypothesis, change one policy or limit, measure lead time and review results in a feedback loop.
Misconception
Incremental doesn't mean aimless. Experiments are small, measurable, and timeboxed for review.
Key Takeaway

Keep roles intact and change the process through small, measured experiments to improve flow safely.

screens.title: Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part B
screens.narratorSegment: The other two Kanban principles focus on people and culture. 'Respect current roles, responsibilities, and titles' means Kanban does not require creating new positions or changing reporting lines as a precondition for improvement. That helps teams adopt Kanban quickly; a content team can keep its editors and writers while introducing a board. 'Encourage acts of leadership at all levels' asks everyone to contribute ideas for improving flow, not just managers. This distributes ownership and surfaces practical improvements from people doing the work. A concrete example is a junior team member proposing a policy to reduce rework in review, then running a small trial. A common mistake is to treat leadership as a title rather than action; leadership in Kanban is about observing flow and proposing small changes. The practical significance is culture: when everyone feels empowered to suggest experiments, improvements compound and the system evolves faster. Your task is to invite low-risk experiments from the team and make sure results are visible and measured. Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part B means keep existing roles intact and foster leadership from everyone to discover practical improvements and sustain change.. In practical terms, respect roles and encourage leadership at all levels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Four Foundational Principles — Part B
Respect roles

Respect current roles, responsibilities, and titles

Kanban minimizes organizational disruption by allowing people to keep their jobs as you add visual workflow and policies.

Example
A content team keeps editors and writers, but adds explicit handover criteria between writing and editing.
Why it helps
Fewer political obstacles to adoption mean quicker gains from visibility and limits.
Encourage leadership

Encourage acts of leadership at all levels

Invite anyone to notice bottlenecks and propose experiments. Leadership is measured by action, not title.

Concrete case
A junior editor suggests a checklist to reduce rework; the team trials it and measures reduced cycle time in Review.
Misconception
Leadership acts are not extra tasks — they're small, focused improvements that improve team flow.
Key Takeaway

Keep people in place and create permission for everyone to propose and test small improvements that improve flow.

screens.title: Visualize the Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Visualizing the workflow is the most visible Kanban practice because it creates the shared reality teams need to manage flow. A typical board uses columns like Backlog, Ready for Dev, In Development, Code Review, In QA, Ready for Release, and Done. The purpose is to make the state of every work item explicit and to reveal bottlenecks. When you design a board, pick between five and seven meaningful stages that reflect actual handoffs in your team. A practical example is a content team mapping Ideas, Writing, Editing, Review, Publishing, and Done. For each column consider whether it needs a WIP limit and whether the entry and exit criteria should be explicit policies. People often make the mistake of creating too many narrow columns; that fragments the workflow and makes flow harder to measure. Instead, aim for clarity: each column should represent a discrete step with clear criteria. Use card annotations for blockers or customer urgency. The board becomes the team’s control panel — inspect it daily and use its signals to prioritize work and drive experiments. Visualize the Workflow means a kanban board visualizes the real workflow; choose 5–7 stages with clear entry and exit criteria to reveal and fix bottlenecks.. In practical terms, designing a practical kanban board. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Visualize the Workflow
Practice

Visualize the Workflow

Design columns that match real handoffs and use cards to represent work items moving left to right.

Board example
Backlog | Ready for Dev | In Development | Code Review | In QA | Ready for Release | Done
Common mistake
Too many micro-columns. That fragments flow and hides where waiting actually happens.
Concrete exercise
List five to seven stages your team actually performs. For each, write the entry and exit criteria. That makes policies explicit and the board actionable.
Key Takeaway
Choose stages that reflect true handoffs and add clear criteria so the board reveals real blockages.
Pro tip
Start broad and split columns later if you need finer visibility.

screens.title: Limit Work In Progress (WIP)
screens.narratorSegment: Limiting Work In Progress is the practice that most directly changes team behavior and reduces multitasking. A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a column. For example, a development column with WIP 3 means only three items can be actively developed at any time. The immediate effect is reduced context switching and a stronger focus on finishing work. WIP limits also make bottlenecks visible: if Testing is full while Development is idle, you know the blockage exists in Testing. One common mistake is setting WIP limits too high, which effectively removes the constraint and yields little benefit. Another error is ignoring violations; consistently breaking the limit hides systemic issues like resource constraints or unclear requirements. A practical scenario: a content team uses Writing (WIP 2) and Editing (WIP 1). Writers cannot push more articles forward until editing clears, which forces swarming or priority decisions. The right WIP limit balances utilization and flow; it is often adjusted by experiment and measured with cycle time improvements. Your next step is to pick one column and propose a WIP limit, then measure its impact for one sprint or two-week window.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Limit Work In Progress (WIP)
Practice

Limit Work In Progress (WIP)

Set explicit maxima for active work in a column so teams focus on finishing before starting new items.

Concrete example
Writing (WIP 2) and Editing (WIP 1). Writers must wait to move work into Editing until the editor has capacity.
Common mistakes
Setting limits too high or failing to enforce them masks flow problems. Treat violations as signals to investigate.
How to choose a limit
Start low and observe. If cycle time increases or idle time grows elsewhere, adjust. Record cycle time before and after the change to measure impact.
Key Takeaway
WIP limits change behavior and reveal real constraints. Use them as experiments, not rigid quotas.
Check your understanding
Which column in your workflow would benefit most from a lower WIP limit right now, and why?

screens.title: Manage Flow with Metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Managing flow means observing how work moves and using simple metrics to make decisions. Lead time measures the total time from commitment to delivery; cycle time measures how long a card spends in a specific stage. These two metrics let you see where delays occur. For example, if lead time is long but cycle time in Development is short, the delay may be in handoffs or waiting for priorities. A content team might see long cycle time in Editing, signaling a bottleneck that needs capacity or a policy change. A common misconception is that throughput alone tells the whole story; throughput ignores where time is spent. Use cycle time histograms or cumulative flow diagrams to spot where work accumulates. When you identify a bottleneck, run a small experiment: change a WIP limit, add a temporary resource, or clarify policies, and then measure lead and cycle time again. The flow management loop is observe, hypothesize, experiment, and measure. Ask yourself: what single metric will tell you whether an experiment improved flow? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Manage Flow with Metrics
Practice

Manage Flow

Measure lead time for end-to-end performance and cycle time for stage-specific delays.

Definitions
Lead time: commitment to delivery. Cycle time: time inside a particular stage.
Example
If Editing cycle time rises, consider adding capacity or clarifying acceptance criteria to reduce rework.
How to act
Use simple charts: cycle time histograms, or a cumulative flow diagram. Spot where work piles up and treat a limit breach as a signal to run an experiment.
Key Takeaway
Metrics make bottlenecks visible. Use them to test hypotheses and measure improvement after experiments.
Check
What metric will show whether your next change made lead time better or worse?

screens.title: Make Policies Explicit and Implement Feedback Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Explicit policies and feedback loops are paired practices that keep Kanban practical and measurable. Policies define how a card moves: entry criteria, exit criteria, handling blocked items, and prioritization rules. For example, an 'In Testing' exit policy could require a passing checklist and no critical bugs. Clear policies reduce ambiguity and speed decisions. Feedback loops—daily stand-ups focused on flow, service delivery reviews, and operations reviews—create regular opportunities to inspect performance and adapt. A common mistake is to write long, vague policies that nobody reads; instead prefer short, testable criteria posted on the board. Use a feedback loop after each small experiment: did cycle time improve? If not, what other change should you try? An actionable sequence: pick a column, write a short definition of done, set a WIP limit, run for two weeks, then review lead and cycle time. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Make Policies Explicit & Feedback Loops
Practice

Make Policies Explicit

Write short, testable rules that define when work may enter or exit a column to remove ambiguity.

Policy example
In Testing entry: passed developer tests and deployed to staging. In Testing exit: all acceptance criteria validated and no critical bugs.
Pitfall
Avoid long, theoretical policies — prefer concise checklists people can follow daily.
Practice

Implement Feedback Loops

Use daily flow-focused stand-ups and periodic service reviews to inspect and adapt based on metrics and observations.

Key Takeaway
Short, frequent reviews and concise policies create a feedback loop that powers continuous improvement.
Try this
Write a one-sentence entry and exit policy for two columns and review them after two iterations.

screens.title: Improve Collaboratively, Evolve Experimentally
screens.narratorSegment: The final Kanban practice ties the principles and practices together: improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally. This is a team-centered scientific approach: propose small changes, run them as experiments, measure the effect, and decide whether to adopt them. For instance, a team noticing long verification times might trial an automated test script for two weeks and measure cycle time before and after. The role of leadership here is to enable experiments, not to dictate them; anyone can propose a trial. A misconception is that experimentation equals instability. Well-designed experiments are small, reversible, and measurable, so they reduce risk while generating learning. Use a short hypothesis format: we believe X change will cause Y improvement in Z metric; we will measure Z for two weeks. If the data supports the hypothesis, adopt the change and make its policy explicit. If not, revert or try another experiment. Over time, many small wins accumulate into significant improvements without the disruption of a large overhaul. Ask: what one small experiment could you run this week to improve a bottleneck you can see on your board?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Improve Collaboratively
Practice

Improve Collaboratively, Evolve Experimentally

Make small, team-led experiments with a hypothesis and measurable metric, then inspect and adapt.

Hypothesis template
We believe changing X will reduce cycle time in Y by Z percent. Measure cycle time for two weeks and compare.
Example
Trial an automated test step for verification. If cycle time in Verification falls, adopt the test and update the policy.
Practical steps
  1. Identify a bottleneck with metrics or the board.
  2. Propose a small, reversible change and define the metric to measure.
  3. Run the experiment for a fixed time and review results together.
Key Takeaway

Small, measured experiments reduce risk and build continuous improvement into daily work.

screens.title: Designing a Kanban Board with WIP Limits (Activity)
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks you through designing a simple Kanban board for a small maintenance and support team. First, define five to seven stages that reflect how work flows, for example: Backlog, Ready for Analysis, In Analysis, Ready for Development, In Development, In Testing, Ready for Deployment, Done. Second, set WIP limits for active stages: Ready for Analysis (WIP 3), In Analysis (WIP 2), In Development (WIP 3), In Testing (WIP 2), Ready for Deployment (WIP 5). These sample numbers balance focus and throughput for a small team. Third, write explicit policies for two columns. For In Analysis: entry requires acceptance by Product and notes on technical approach; exit requires estimates and clear acceptance criteria. The exercise emphasizes measurable changes: run the board for two cycles, track cycle time per column, and adjust limits based on observed bottlenecks. What one column will you limit first and why?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Designing a Kanban Board (Activity)

Activity: Design a Kanban Board with WIP Limits

Follow these steps to design a practical board for a small maintenance and support team.

1. Define workflow stages
Example stages: Backlog | Ready for Analysis | In Analysis | Ready for Development | In Development | In Testing | Ready for Deployment | Done

Design boards and limits around real handoffs, test changes, and use data to guide further adjustments.

fullNarratorScript:
Kanban is a lightweight, practical approach to managing knowledge work that started in manufacturing and found a powerful second life in software and services. In this lesson you will learn why Kanban focuses on visualizing the workflow, limiting how much is in progress, and improving the way work flows from request to delivery. We will connect the four foundational principles — starting with what you do now, evolutionary change, respecting roles, and encouraging leadership at all levels — to six actionable practices like visualizing the board and setting WIP limits. You will see concrete examples, such as a content team's board, and common misconceptions, for instance thinking that WIP limits are the same as arbitrary quotas. By the end, you will understand when Kanban is a better fit than a time-boxed framework and how small experiments can move your team toward smoother delivery. Keep an eye on the visual cards illustrating board stages, WIP, and a traffic metaphor to build an intuitive picture of flow.

In this set of objectives you will see four specific, verifiable skills to target while learning Kanban. First, you will explain Kanban's origins and its core philosophy, which helps ground the practices in a real-world context and shows why visualizing flow matters. Second, you will identify and describe the four foundational principles of Kanban so you can evaluate how a team culture supports evolutionary change. Third, you will understand and apply the six core practices, with emphasis on visualizing workflow and limiting Work In Progress; these practices form the toolkit for daily use. Fourth, you will learn to differentiate Kanban from Scrum, noticing how continuous flow contrasts with time-boxed Sprints and what that difference means for planning and cadence. Each objective links a clear skill to a practical reason: you will be able to design a board, set WIP limits, and choose the right approach for your team. As you study, look for opportunities to practice small experiments rather than trying to change everything at once.

This second objectives slide moves from knowing to doing. You will learn to design a Kanban board with appropriate WIP limits for a small maintenance or support team, which is a practical, hands-on skill. You will also make policies explicit for key columns, such as Definition of Done for analysis or testing, which reduces ambiguity and helps flow. Additionally, you will practice using metrics like lead time and cycle time to identify bottlenecks and measure the effect of small experiments. Finally, you will be able to recognize scenarios that favor Kanban — unpredictable incoming requests, continuous delivery needs, or teams that cannot reassign roles easily — and justify the choice. Each objective pairs a clear action with a reason, so you can both build and defend a Kanban design in typical workplace situations.

Kanban began as a scheduling system in Toyota's production system and later translated into knowledge work because of its focus on flow and visual control. At its core Kanban is a method to make work visible, constrain work in progress, and encourage incremental improvement. The philosophy is intentionally non-prescriptive: you start with your current process and evolve it, rather than ripping everything up and replacing roles. A concrete example is a software operations team that maps incident handling to a board and then adds limits so they finish incidents faster. A common misconception is that Kanban is merely a to-do board; it's not. The board is a diagnostic tool used with policies, metrics, and experiments to improve flow. In practice, you'll notice that the same card moving slowly through stages signals different problems: lack of skill in a stage, unclear acceptance criteria, or resource shortages. The takeaway is that Kanban pairs simple visual tools with evidence-based changes — you visualize to learn, then experiment and measure, and encourage leadership across the team to propose improvements. How might you start by mapping one process you use today?

Two of Kanban's most distinctive principles help teams adopt changes with minimal disruption. First, 'Start with what you do now' asks you to map your existing workflow, roles, and responsibilities without requiring immediate structural changes. The practical benefit is lower resistance: team members keep their roles and still gain visibility. For example, a support team might leave existing escalation paths in place while introducing a simple board to track incoming tickets. Second, 'Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change' emphasizes making small, measurable experiments rather than large overhauls. A concrete experiment could be changing a WIP limit for one column to see whether lead time improves. A common error is to misread evolutionary change as slow or vague; in fact it's deliberate and measurable. Each small change should have a hypothesis, a way to measure lead or cycle time, and a review loop. These two principles combined make Kanban adoptable in environments where stability of roles is important, and they prioritize learning over assumption. Think of each experiment as a tiny scientific trial: small, safe, and information-rich. Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part A means begin with the current process and make deliberate, incremental changes measured by simple metrics.. In practical terms, start with what you do now and pursue evolutionary change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The other two Kanban principles focus on people and culture. 'Respect current roles, responsibilities, and titles' means Kanban does not require creating new positions or changing reporting lines as a precondition for improvement. That helps teams adopt Kanban quickly; a content team can keep its editors and writers while introducing a board. 'Encourage acts of leadership at all levels' asks everyone to contribute ideas for improving flow, not just managers. This distributes ownership and surfaces practical improvements from people doing the work. A concrete example is a junior team member proposing a policy to reduce rework in review, then running a small trial. A common mistake is to treat leadership as a title rather than action; leadership in Kanban is about observing flow and proposing small changes. The practical significance is culture: when everyone feels empowered to suggest experiments, improvements compound and the system evolves faster. Your task is to invite low-risk experiments from the team and make sure results are visible and measured. Four Foundational Principles of Kanban — Part B means keep existing roles intact and foster leadership from everyone to discover practical improvements and sustain change.. In practical terms, respect roles and encourage leadership at all levels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Visualizing the workflow is the most visible Kanban practice because it creates the shared reality teams need to manage flow. A typical board uses columns like Backlog, Ready for Dev, In Development, Code Review, In QA, Ready for Release, and Done. The purpose is to make the state of every work item explicit and to reveal bottlenecks. When you design a board, pick between five and seven meaningful stages that reflect actual handoffs in your team. A practical example is a content team mapping Ideas, Writing, Editing, Review, Publishing, and Done. For each column consider whether it needs a WIP limit and whether the entry and exit criteria should be explicit policies. People often make the mistake of creating too many narrow columns; that fragments the workflow and makes flow harder to measure. Instead, aim for clarity: each column should represent a discrete step with clear criteria. Use card annotations for blockers or customer urgency. The board becomes the team’s control panel — inspect it daily and use its signals to prioritize work and drive experiments. In practical terms, designing a practical kanban board. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Limiting Work In Progress is the practice that most directly changes team behavior and reduces multitasking. A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a column. For example, a development column with WIP 3 means only three items can be actively developed at any time. The immediate effect is reduced context switching and a stronger focus on finishing work. WIP limits also make bottlenecks visible: if Testing is full while Development is idle, you know the blockage exists in Testing. One common mistake is setting WIP limits too high, which effectively removes the constraint and yields little benefit. Another error is ignoring violations; consistently breaking the limit hides systemic issues like resource constraints or unclear requirements. A practical scenario: a content team uses Writing (WIP 2) and Editing (WIP 1). Writers cannot push more articles forward until editing clears, which forces swarming or priority decisions. The right WIP limit balances utilization and flow; it is often adjusted by experiment and measured with cycle time improvements. Your next step is to pick one column and propose a WIP limit, then measure its impact for one sprint or two-week window.

Managing flow means observing how work moves and using simple metrics to make decisions. Lead time measures the total time from commitment to delivery; cycle time measures how long a card spends in a specific stage. These two metrics let you see where delays occur. For example, if lead time is long but cycle time in Development is short, the delay may be in handoffs or waiting for priorities. A content team might see long cycle time in Editing, signaling a bottleneck that needs capacity or a policy change. A common misconception is that throughput alone tells the whole story; throughput ignores where time is spent. Use cycle time histograms or cumulative flow diagrams to spot where work accumulates. When you identify a bottleneck, run a small experiment: change a WIP limit, add a temporary resource, or clarify policies, and then measure lead and cycle time again. The flow management loop is observe, hypothesize, experiment, and measure. Ask yourself: what single metric will tell you whether an experiment improved flow? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
